title: Senior's toolkit: finding your way
summary: ls, find, rg, type -a, df and du: find files, find text and find where the disk went on a server you have never seen.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: finding your way
steps.body: On a new server you need to answer three questions fast: where are the files, which program actually runs, and where did the disk space go.

toolkit.what: A long listing with sizes people can read, hidden files included, newest last, so the file that just changed is right above your prompt.
flags: long format: permissions, owner, size, time

toolkit.what: Jumps back to the previous directory. `pushd` and `popd` keep a stack when you bounce between more than two.
flags: go somewhere and come back later

toolkit.what: Finds files by name, type, age or size, then can act on each one.
flags: changed in the last hour / day
run a command on all matches at once
toolkit.when: "what changed on this box in the last hour?"

toolkit.what: ripgrep: searches file contents recursively, fast, and skips what `.gitignore` ignores.
Shows every command with that name on your PATH, plus aliases and functions, in the order the shell tries them.
flags: all matches, not just the first
the script-friendly form: prints the path or fails
toolkit.when: "I installed the new version but the old one runs"

toolkit.what: Free space per filesystem. `-i` shows inodes: a disk can be "full" with space left when millions of tiny files use up every inode.
Which folder is eating the disk, biggest last. Repeat one level down until you find it.
flags: stay on one filesystem (skip /proc and mounts)
toolkit.when: an alert says the disk is 95% full

steps.prompt: Match each `find` test to its meaning.
pairs: run a command on all matches

steps.prompt: You installed Python 3.12 into `/usr/local/bin`, but `python3 --version` still prints 3.9. What do you run first?
options: `type -a python3` to see every `python3` on the PATH and which comes first
steps.explain: The shell runs the first match in PATH order (or an alias). `type -a` lists them all, so you see whether `/usr/bin` comes before `/usr/local/bin`, or an alias is in the way. Running `hash -r` clears the shell's cached location.

steps.prompt: An alert says `/var` is 100% full, but `df -h` shows 2 GB free and writes still fail with `No space left on device`. What do you check?
options: `df -i /var`: the inodes may be used up by millions of small files
steps.explain: Every file needs an inode. A runaway job writing tiny session or cache files can use them all while bytes remain free. Then `find /var -xdev -type f | cut -d/ -f2,3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -n` shows where they are.

steps.prompt: Show which folders under `/var` use the most space, biggest last, without crossing into other filesystems.
steps.explain: `-x` stays on one filesystem. `sort -h` understands `512K` < `3G`; `sort -n` would put `3G` before `512K` because it only reads the digits.

steps.prompt: Which tool do you reach for?
items: Every file changed in `/etc` in the last day
Where an error message is defined in the source
Is any filesystem out of inodes

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: On any unfamiliar server, start with `df -h`, `ls -lahtr` on the folder you care about and `find -mmin` for recent changes. Install `rg` wherever you are allowed to; it turns a five-minute grep into a second.
